_comment_family: Anton asked for at 700 — a weight this family DOES NOT HAVE as a
file, which is the whole of what makes this pack unusual and the
reason it is this long. Read it before setting anything else in it.
Anton is a single-weight family by design. There is one cut, it is
the Regular in fonts/, and there is no bold of it to ship: a channel
asking to pick its words out in 'Anton Bold' cannot be handed a
second file the way hall-of-femme is handed Telegraf's 200 and 800.
So this face is the same file asked for by a heavier name, and the
The family is 'Anton' and not an alias, and that is what does the
work. The stylesheet declares 'Anton' at font-weight 400 (see
styles.css) and nothing else on the machine answers to the name, so a
canvas asking for `700 40px "Anton"` matches that one 400 face and
Blink emboldens its outlines itself. Synthetic bold, in other words,
requested deliberately and by the only route there is.
_comment_safety: Why that is not the failure fontguard exists to catch, and why it
would be one under almost any other circumstance.
The thing fontguard is guarding against is a block laid out against
one face's metrics and drawn in another's — a title composed against
numbers that describe a font nobody can see. Nothing of that kind
happens here, because there is only ever one file. The measurement
and the draw go through the same font string (see `styleFor` and
`textProps` in js/text.js), so whatever the browser does to the
outlines it does to both halves at once: the advances a row is
stacked and broken on come back from the same call that paints it.
One caveat, and it is worth a sentence rather than a footnote. An
emboldened glyph is the 400 stroked outward, so it can spill a
fraction of a pixel past the ink bounds measured for it — a box
padded to a picked word therefore sits a hair tighter than the same
box round a word in a real bold cut would. At 40px on a box padded by
about five that is under a pixel, and it is a box, not a line break.
What this face must NOT be asked to carry is a highlight that is
weight and nothing else. Anton is already a heavy condensed display
face; stroking it outward by a fraction of its own weight is a
refinement, not a step somebody reads from across a room. The one
channel set in it picks its words out in near-black on a yellow box
and the weight is the third thing that changes, not the first (see
conspiracy-central). A channel wanting weight to be the highlight
should reach for a family that has two real cuts, the way
hall-of-femme does.
fontguard keys its check by family, so this face and anton.json
share one answer rather than being verified separately. That is
correct here for the same reason all of the above is: they are one
file, and verifying 'Anton' verifies both of them.

_comment_local: What the machine may already know the face by. Unused while `css` is
true — the stylesheet's own declaration carries the same two local()

_comment_stack: The fallbacks are damage limitation and never a design choice: a
title laid out against the wrong metrics is broken rather than merely
different, which is what fontguard exists to catch before it is ever
drawn. Impact and Arial Black behind it because Anton is a heavy
condensed display cut and those are the nearest things a Windows
machine is certain to have. The same stack as anton.json, for the
reason `local` above is the same list.
